title: Lesson 8: Configuration: Models, Providers, and Fallbacks: Why It Works on My Machine Isn't Enough
description: The consultant's configuration discipline: keeping model and provider separate, secrets out of settings, verifying what the running agent actually resolved, and building a fallback chain so the client's agent survives a provider outage.

questions.question: Why keep model and provider as separate configuration keys?
options: So the model file stays small and easy to copy
So the provider can be swapped without changing the model
So secrets can be stored in the same file as the settings
So the agent always uses the most expensive model available
questions.explanation: Separate keys let you swap the provider to survive an outage, or swap the model to tune cost, without touching the other.

questions.question: If you never verify which settings the running agent honors, why is 'it works on my machine' a problem?
options: The agent may work only because of settings absent elsewhere
The install always rewrites the config file it reads
A running agent ignores the config file entirely
Secrets in the environment are always overridden by defaults
questions.explanation: Configuration is resolved through layers that can override your file, so only the behavior the running agent shows is real evidence.

questions.question: What does a configured fallback chain do when the primary provider starts returning errors?
options: It permanently switches the agent over to the backup model
It swaps in place, keeping history, then reverts next turn
It stops the agent until a human restarts the primary
It re-runs the failed request without the conversation history
questions.explanation: The fallback swaps model and provider in place while keeping the conversation, then returns to the primary on the next turn.
